Ingredients

2 lbs of Ground beef

Vegetable Oil

Crushed garlic

Half of an onion (Red of white) Diced

Salt

Pepper 1 Packet of taco seasoning.

Flour Tortillas

Iceberg Lettuce

1 Tomato

1 cup of Jack or Cheddar cheese grated

Sour Cream Salsa

Method

In a large saucepan add one teaspoon of Oil and heat on medium. Once your pan is hot, add your Onions and one clove of Garlic. Cook until the garlic starts to turn brown. Then add your hamburger meat. Sprinkle lightly with Salt and Pepper.

Stir frequently and cook until the meat has browned. Next dump into a strainer in the sink to strain out the excess grease and then transfer back to the pan.

Add 3/4 of a cup of water to the meat and the contents of the Taco Seasoning packet. Mix well, when it starts bubbling turn the heat down to simmer.

While your meat is finishing warm your tortillas on a hot flat non stick pan and put them between two folded dish towels to keep warm.

Stir your meat again,, it should slowly start to get thicker as the water boils off.

Chop up your tomato's and Lettuce.

Once the juice in the meat has the consistency of honey, turn if off it's done.

Assemble your taco's and enjoy!!

Here's a story about a friend of mine.

Back in the early 90s, I lived in a shitty trailer park. There were a bunch of kids living in the area, so we would all get together and play outside a lot. Thing was, the boys and the girls usually played separately - boys wanted to play sports and such, girls wanted to play pretend. That sort of thing, you know how little kids are. Except this one girl, who we will call Jane for the sake of this story. She was a total tomboy, and to be honest, she was tougher than all the boys, possibly put together. She was really fit and had short hair as well. She ran faster, jumped higher, could beat us up and wasn't the slightest bit girly. We'd get a scraped knee? We'd cry. Her? She'd just walk it off. She was the toughest chick I've ever known.

Well, one day, we're all riding bikes around the neighborhood and decide to stop at the corner store and buy some ice cream and stuff. We're all sitting around in front of the store, eating our snacks, and someone points out that Jane looks a little sick. She insisted that she was fine, she was just tired. Some of the boys mocked her and said that her girliness was catching up with her and everyone was laughing. So she stands up like she's gonna beat him up for insulting her... and then she falls down onto the pavement, clutching her chest and screaming.

The clerk comes out of the store, sees whats going on and calls the ambulance.

She was in the hospital for a few weeks, and nobody was allowed to visit her. When she finally came home, you could tell that she wasn't the same at all. Her eyes looked dead and lifeless. Like she had no hope left. It turned out that she had some sort of heart condition, and even minor exertion could trigger another heart attack and she could die. She wasn't allowed to play outside anymore. She wasn't allowed to get excited about anything. Her parents forced her to stay in the house every day and read and such. She wasn't even allowed to play video games because it might excite her too much. We all came to visit her often, but we never stayed long. There was an air of sadness, and quite frankly, we were bored to be around her.

Fast forward a few months, and her family decides that they're going to move in with her grandparents. They had a big house in the country or something, and it would be "more relaxing" for her to be there. So they leave town, and I assumed I would never see her again. To be honest, it probably would have been better if I hadn't, but I did.

Fast forward to when I was 24. I'm living in a new town, got my own shitty job and my own shitty apartment, but doing okay for myself. I go to the nearby Wal Mart, and when I'm checking out, the cashier says "Oh hey! Are you (my name)?" and I had no idea who she was. Then I read her nametag, Jane. Yes, it was the same girl. But you would never have known it from looking at her.

She was severely overweight - borderline obese. Her hair was long and unkempt, and she just overall looked to not be taking care of herself. I asked her how she had been. Terrible, of course. She was still suffering from this condition, and she had had several near-death heart attacks over the past several years. She was lucky to be alive. She asked me if I wanted to grab a bite to eat, but I had stuff to do, so I told her that I'd catch up with her later and got her phone number.

The following day, I met up with her at her house - she was living with her mother at the time. The house was a house of filth, with trash and bugs everywhere. I didn't want to be rude, so I didn't say anything about it. We left and went to lunch at Denny's and even though it was supposed to be this exciting reuniting of old friends, she still seemed just as lifeless as before. Partway through the meal, she completely broke down in tears. She told me about all the dreams she had as a child, all the things she wanted to do with her life, and how it was all stolen from her. At the end of it all, she said "I've been dead since I was 10 years old." (which was when she was diagnosed). And then she collapsed onto the table. She had a heart attack and died right there.

I just shared this on another post, but it fits here too.

My father is an alcoholic. He has bounced between sobriety and drink for years. With his longest period of sobriety taking place during my middle school to beginning of high school years. After that he really never had more than a week or two sober. He was always a "functioning drunk" but I hate that term. He basically kept a girlfriend, car, dream job (building guitars for himself and Gibson) and roof over his head. What some may call the basics. During this time period we really didn't have a relationship due to past struggles and conflict between us. Also he lived in another town a few hours away; out of sight, out of mind.

Moving on to grown up me, I got married and had a child while he lost everything after not leaving his room for months, drinking solid. This hit me hard. I personally felt bad for not moving past the previous bullshit and getting to know him better before he got that bad. I started to make myself present more so he knew I was there for him. I even drove to his home hours away, without him knowing, on a chance to see him and talk. It was kind of like an intervention but it was just me and him. Fast forward a few months and he moved to my city, went into treatment, moved into a sober living house and got a job he said he really liked. He was doing great for 6 months. He was a father and a grandfather. Then, I feel, he gave it up. Now he is officially homeless. At this point he has been officially homeless for 3-4 days.

This is where the hard choice came into play. He showed up drunk at my work, I took his bottle of vodka and dumped it. He waited for me at my house after work. I had stuff to do after work so he sat there for hours waiting. We talked and he left. Then he came back and asked to stay. I know I made the right choice by telling him no, but it still has been the hardest thing I have had to do yet. He got a look on his face that was full of so much sadness. I have never seen something like that before on him or anyone. He left. I couldn't leave him like that. I called around and found a local program that could possibly take him in for the night. After finding him on a park bench I took him down there, helped him fill out the needed paperwork and saw him right "homeless" on paper for the first time.

I had a friend growing up who was really tall and strong for his age (at about 12 he looked like a fairly strong adult) and was good at sports and wanted to pursue a career in it, and probably could have gotten a scholarship. In high school he got a collapsed lung playing football, so he had to quit that and he really fucked up by getting caught with drug paraphernalia while skipping class.

He also had parents who didn't enforce anything and were distant. One day (I can't remember if it was before or after getting caught) he got into a fight with his dad. It started out verbal and then he just punched his dad in the face. Last time I talked with my friend (two years ago) he told me that he hadn't really talked with his dad in a while. He also told me he was still on parole.

I had a great conversation with him though, and he knows a lot of things, but I feel bad that he doesn't have a positive outlook on life. He told me that he thinks that he will be dead by 30.

One good thing came out of him really screwing up though: his brother has decided to not follow in his brother's footsteps like he used to do.

It's tough ground to cover, either way. Especially given all the "free for life" marketing that has occurred thus far.
